photographs.prompt:
Edit the FIRST input photograph. One full-bleed photographic image, wide 2.098:1, same camera and composition for a print gardening book. INPUT 1 is the base photograph for this exact first step. INPUT 2 is a three-view contact sheet of REAL CAMERA photographs of the man in the scene: very important for reshaping his jaw and chin faithfully. INPUT 3 supplies his actual cool-weather clothing only. This is one Cornish late-autumn afternoon, outdoors after a light shower, with cool overcast soft grey light, slight damp sheen on a few leaves and the tarp but no pouring rain or puddles. The picture will be paired with a warm sunny view taken the following late spring.
Keep John kneeling on the grass on the right, lowering the final brick onto the near right hem of a flat fully opaque, ordinary dark forest-green woven tarpaulin. Match his two hands on the brick, the ordinary perimeter weights, the existing layout and perspective of the tarp, his charcoal jumper, dark blue jeans and work shoes. Keep the fence, its worn low wall and the tiny slice at far right of his glass greenhouse on a pale grey brick plinth. Same understated, matter-of-fact photograph with comfortable headroom. NO shed.
The owner asks for a proper established lawn. REPLACE ALL the sparse, coarse and muddy ground visible OUTSIDE the edges of the tarp and under the actor with dense, closed, lush short mown lawn, attractive but authentic Cornish grass, mixed fine blades close together. A living continuous carpet with no earth peeking through it, right up to the tarpaulin, visible in front, along each side and behind. A few discreet recognisable flat dandelion, clover or plantain rosettes growing low in that lawn, especially near a tarp corner, testify to the weedy area, not an overgrown meadow. Leave the cover intact, flat and fully covering the treatment area with no dead weeds arranged on it. Subtle late-autumn clues only e.g. a couple of small fallen leaves at the fence, subdued greens; don't drown the details or darken the face.
Correct John's likeness using the real close views in the SECOND input as the authority. Match the slimmer taper in his lower cheeks, the small softly rounded and slightly set-back chin, his short mixed grey beard following his skin, softer natural jaw-to-neck transition. In particular bring back the protruding lower outline relative to the lower lip seen in the base, so it doesn't jut forward, square off, or appear reinforced by a shadow or by a thick block of beard. A relaxed mature man concentrating on the brick, still the same John, his natural forehead, hairline, nose and expression. Keep the downward gaze but let sufficient three-quarter part profile be seen to read the actual jaw contour. Understated documentary realism, normal texture, one image only, no typography or collage.

Precisely localised retouch of the FIRST photograph, single native wide frame 1816x866. The overall location is now close. Fix the remaining rear LEFT corner and rear/right clearance using the real before/after site constraint. Input 2 is the previous season's tarp. Both pictures must show the very same small rectangle of lawn over the same fence-post bay. Input 3 is an accurately registered silhouette of the exact target patch in camera 1 coordinates. It deliberately marks the feet of the two fixed posts. This is not artwork to reproduce; in the result every edge is a normal grassy edge.
1. Look specifically at the far-left junction in input 1. It presently lies virtually off-frame, several feet to the left of the first post, and the bed's left edge is almost vertical. This is wrong. Grow green lawn into that far left triangle so the uncovered rectangle becomes more clearly FORESHORTENED and tapered on the left, like the silhouette in input 3. Place its rear-left corner at x=112 to 118 pixels (6.3% of the width) and y=444 pixels (51.3% height). That is a few inches in front of and just LEFT of the very FIRST vertical concrete post (post centre about x=160). The target left edge slopes down and to the LEFT from that corner to the near-left corner at the lower left edge of frame, around x=3,y=852. This creates a visible triangular wedge of lovely green grass on the left of the plot that is wider at the rear.
2. Follow rear edge from that corrected corner to rear-right at about x=912 y=364, a few inches in front of and just to the RIGHT of the next post at x=860. Both posts must visibly stand entirely in GREEN GRASS and a narrow, unbroken 25–35 pixel deep grassy strip must separate the bottom of the rear wall from the dark earth, all along the back. This small gap is visible in the autumn photo; do not let the back edge touch either concrete post. Make that rear soil/lawn edge run parallel to the foot of the wall. Keep the near right corner by the rake, the rake teeth on dead ground, entire near edge near lower border slightly receding to the right. The third reference gives the numeric corners as a drawing.
3. This edit ONLY corrects the perimeter of the brown rectangle. Preserve the first reference almost exactly elsewhere. Preserve actor and softer chin, easy upright pose, clothes, entire balanced rake and the soft brown dead turf texture and real small snag at teeth, camera, lighting, folded tarp and bricks on RIGHT, fence and greenhouse. Do not add a second area, wooden edging, labels, guide lines or borders. Keep the dark and light speckle of the grass and soil natural all along the adjusted seams. Retain the base spring shot's framing; NOT the autumn shot's angle or clothes. Output the complete clean photograph.

visual_research.source: University of Minnesota Turfgrass Science, Gary Deters, Figure 3
visual_research.observation: Direct lawn example after removing an opaque tarp: bare ground mixed with brown vegetation in irregular low patches. Some violets survived in this trial.

visual_research.source: Winterizing Garden Beds, Tarping to Reduce Tillage, p. 8
visual_research.observation: Three-frame bed sequence showing brown residual growth and exposed soil as the cover is pulled back.

edit: Match the exposed ground to the earlier tarp footprint, registered against the fence posts and low wall. Store the tarp and weights to the right.

landmark_registration.basis: The autumn tarp spans one fence bay with narrow grass behind, back corners just outboard of the two posts. Visual registration to the spring viewpoint. Corner positions are estimates, not surveyed coordinates.

first_pass.prompt:
A location continuity correction to one book photograph. Produce exactly ONE full-bleed spring photograph, approximately 2.098:1 landscape.
FIRST INPUT is the spring photo to edit: keep its viewpoint, fence posts, masonry, greenhouse, John standing relaxed with the olive T-shirt and shorts, centred rake joint and real matted brown turf texture. It has the area of dead turf in the WRONG position. SECOND INPUT shows the authoritative real position of the patch in this narrative: the autumn tarp on the grass, tucked near the back wall between identifiable fence posts. Several months later the exposed ground MUST mark the exact place that tarp had covered. THIRD INPUT is a precisely registered POSITION/MASK GUIDE viewed through the spring camera; its brown quadrilateral is the required entire footprint of dead ground. The light and dark strips and two vertical markers are registration with the fence, low wall, and two posts in the spring view. Do not draw this diagram or any outlines; replace its colours with real photographic textures.
Please adhere to these very specific visual checks:
• The far edge of the uncovered bed runs PARALLEL and very close to the low wall under the timber fence. From this oblique camera height it slopes up to the right in the image with only a slim continuous ribbon of green lawn between the wall's foot and the far edge (about half a brick's LENGTH in depth, never a broad strip of spare lawn). Its far LEFT corner lies just in front of, and slightly LEFT of, the first visible fence post; its far RIGHT corner lies just in front of, and slightly RIGHT of, the second visible fence post. The back edge spans this entire bay, not half of it. In normalized image coordinates the corners are approximately back-left (6%,51%), back-right (50%,42%), front-right (74%,89%), front-left (0%,98%). Keep the same wall/ground junction and perspective as reference 1. The near edge is nearly all visible diagonally across the foreground with a narrow ribbon of fresh GRASS in front, especially on the right. This is a rectangle in the ground plane and therefore a trapezoid in the image. It is the rectangular outline left by a removed groundsheet, with modest soft ragged edges, no border or raised lip.
• Put the folded tarp and the bricks fully on the unused GREEN GRASS to the RIGHT of the bed's far right corner, between that corner and the greenhouse, behind and aside from John's work. Leave the full far edge of the exposed bed visible so its alignment with the fence can be read. Do not let the tarp or weights take up their former positions at the rear left and push the bed forward. Maintain a natural mown lawn elsewhere. The spring gap to the right of this bed goes to the greenhouse on its original pale brick base, cropped on the right edge. No blue shed.
• Keep all of John's latest easy upright posture, relaxed feet close together at the RIGHT edge on the lawn, soft chin, olive summer clothes and good tool geometry. Same late spring light. Set the correctly centred metal rake head a few inches inside the soil if needed to keep the teeth gently catching the fine flattened grey-brown dead lawn fibres near the near-right corner. Do not put the head on the green grass or deepen his stance.
• Match the previous brown ground's weathered irregular dead grass felt and patchy undug dark soil, not big leaves or piles. Replace the old mislocated area in its entirety with new correctly located surface and healthy outside lawn. No graphics or marker lines. DO NOT copy ref 2's exact camera angle, clothing, kneeling pose or spread-out tarp. Use only its position relative to the two posts. This is a clean photorealistic minimal edit of reference 1 with the whole patch in the right place. Full rectangular image with no border.
